title: The bystander effect: why do people in a crowd sometimes not help?
examples: Why do people not help when others are around?
How can I be an upstander?

explain.say: Here is a puzzle: if someone falls ill, are you more likely to get help with lots of people around, or just one? Most of us guess lots of people. But scientists found the opposite. Look at the bars. They come from a famous 1968 experiment in New York.

explain.say: See the first bar, alone? Students in the study heard someone over an intercom seem to have a seizure. When each student thought they were the only one listening, 85 out of 100 went to help. That is the tall bar. Would you have helped?

items.label: Alone
items.ask: What happened when people were alone in the experiment?

items.label: With 4 others
items.ask: Why did fewer people help in bigger groups?

explain.say: Now look at the other bars. When students thought one other person was listening, 62 percent helped. With four others, only 31 percent did. See how the bars shrink as the crowd grows? This is the bystander effect: the more people watch, the less likely any one of them helps. Why might that be?

items.label: With 4 others
items.ask: Why did fewer people help in bigger groups?

explain.say: One reason is diffusion of responsibility, a big phrase that means the job of helping feels spread out, so each person thinks someone else will do it. People also look around, see others doing nothing, and decide it must not be serious. Can you see the link with copying others?

explain.say: The good news: once you know about it, you can beat it. Be an upstander: do not wait, point at one person and say "You, please call for help", or tell a trusted adult. A 2019 study of real street videos found that in 9 out of 10 conflicts, at least one person stepped in. Well done! Challenge: learn your local emergency number today.

faq.a: The bystander effect is when people are less likely to help someone in trouble because other people are around. Each person feels less responsible and waits for someone else to act.

faq.q: What happened when people were alone in the experiment?
faq.a: In Darley and Latané's 1968 study, students who thought they were the only one hearing someone have a seizure helped 85 percent of the time, and quickly.
asks: What was the Darley and Latane experiment?

faq.q: Why did fewer people help in bigger groups?
faq.a: With four other listeners, only 31 percent helped. Responsibility felt shared out, so each person assumed someone else would act. This is called diffusion of responsibility.

faq.q: Why do people look at others before helping?
faq.a: When unsure, we check other people's reactions. If everyone looks calm, we decide nothing is wrong, even if everyone else is doing the same thing. This is social proof at work.
asks: Is the bystander effect social proof?

faq.q: How can I be an upstander?
faq.a: Notice, decide it is your job, and act safely: call for help, speak to the person, or point at someone specific and ask them to call. If it feels unsafe, get a trusted adult or call your emergency number.
asks: What should I do in an emergency crowd?

facts: Darley and Latané (1968) found 85 percent of participants helped when alone, 62 percent with one other bystander and 31 percent with four others.
A 2019 study by Philpot and colleagues of 219 real public conflicts filmed in the UK, the Netherlands and South Africa found at least one bystander intervened in about 9 out of 10.

quiz.say: In the 1968 study, when were people most likely to help?
quiz.show: People helped most when they were…
quiz.why: 85 percent helped when they thought they were the only one who could.

wrong.1: With one other person, help dropped to 62 percent.

quiz.say: Someone falls in a busy street. What is a good upstander move?

options.show: Point at one person and ask them to call for help
options.say: Point at one person and ask them to call for help

quiz.why: Giving one person a clear job beats diffusion of responsibility.

wrong.0: If everyone waits, nobody helps; that is the bystander effect.
wrong.2: Walking away leaves the person without help.
